name: Glycopyrrolate (oral)

lead: Oral glycopyrrolate is a prescription pill used off-label for excessive sweating, and some users take it to keep skin and clothing dry and look more composed.

It blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, which reduces sweat and saliva, and it does not cross into the brain easily. Dermatology sources list it among tablets used for hyperhidrosis, and reference works note oral and topical forms for gustatory and generalised sweating. Registered studies of the oral form for sweating are few and small.

paras: It is taken as a tablet under medical direction, and the drying effect is felt within days. It is often used for sweating that covers more than one area, such as the whole body.
Dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision and reduced sweating leading to heat prostration are listed. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Oral glycopyrrolate is used off-label for excessive sweating, and some users take it to keep skin and clothing dry and look more composed. It blocks the signal that tells sweat glands to work, so less sweat reaches skin and clothes. Registered studies of the oral form for sweating are few and small.

lead: Glycopyrrolate, also called glycopyrronium bromide, is a prescription anticholinergic tablet and solution that reduces sweating and saliva. People who sweat heavily through the face, underarms, palms or whole body use it to keep skin dry, avoid visible sweat marks on clothing and keep makeup and hair in place, which is why it appears in skin and appearance discussions.[1][2][3]

It is a synthetic quaternary-ammonium muscarinic antagonist that acts mainly outside the brain and can be given by mouth, injection, topically or by inhalation. It has been used since 1961, first for peptic ulcer.[1] Dermatology reviews group oral glycopyrrolate with other oral anticholinergics for severe hyperhidrosis, describing them as useful adjuncts when other treatments fail.[3][4][5]

A separate topical product, glycopyrronium tosylate cloths, was approved by the US FDA in 2018 for underarm sweating, described as the first drug developed specifically for that purpose.[1][1] The oral form discussed here is a prescription-only medicine in the US, Canada, the UK and the EU.[1]

paras: Authorised uses vary by formulation and country. Reported uses include peptic ulcer, reducing secretions before anaesthesia (since 1975), drooling (sialorrhea), Meniere's disease and, in inhaled form, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.[1][6] It is also given with neostigmine to counter that drug's slowing of the heart. Inhaled doses are much lower than oral ones, so a swallowed inhaled dose has little effect.[1]

Hyperhidrosis is sweating beyond what body temperature regulation requires. Wikipedia says focal hyperhidrosis may affect up to about 2.8 percent of the US population, usually begins in adolescence in its primary form and runs in families, and that over 80 percent of patients report moderate to severe emotional effects; commonly described consequences include avoiding handshakes, changing shirts often and difficulty with some shoes and jobs.[2] Secondary hyperhidrosis can follow other conditions or medications such as SSRIs.[2]

A review in American Family Physician defines hyperhidrosis as excessive sweating that affects quality of life and causes social and work impairment and emotional distress, and places topical aluminium chloride first in most cases of primary focal hyperhidrosis, topical glycopyrrolate first-line for craniofacial sweating, botulinum toxin as first- or second-line, iontophoresis for palms and soles, and oral anticholinergics as adjuncts in severe cases when other treatments fail.[5]

The American Academy of Dermatology describes oral glycopyrronium and oxybutynin as reducing sweating throughout the body, taken temporarily before an event or continued as needed at the lowest effective dose. Other options it lists include prescription antiperspirants, glycopyrronium cloths, sofpironium gel, botulinum toxin, iontophoresis and microwave thermolysis.[7] Wikipedia's treatment ladder likewise lists antiperspirants, iontophoresis, oral anticholinergics including glycopyrrolate, botulinum toxin, sympathectomy and the miraDry microwave device.[2]

sections.h: Where it sits among sweating treatments
paras: Wikipedia's hyperhidrosis article describes a ladder of options. Prescription-strength aluminium-based antiperspirants are usually tried first and take about three to five days to take effect; tap-water iontophoresis is used for hands and feet, with one trial reporting around an 80 percent reduction in sweating; and botulinum toxin injections, FDA-approved for severe underarm sweating, last roughly three to nine months.[2] Oral anticholinergics such as glycopyrrolate and oxybutynin are described as helpful, with dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation and visual disturbance as the usual trade-offs, and surgery (endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy) is reserved for severe cases because compensatory sweating elsewhere affects an estimated 20 to 80 percent of patients.[2]

Because oral glycopyrrolate acts on the whole body, dermatology guidance frames it as suited to generalised or multi-site sweating, or to sweating that has not responded to local measures, while treatments applied to the skin target one area.[7][5] The American Academy of Dermatology says the tablets can be taken temporarily before an event or continued as needed at the lowest effective amount.[7]

Glycopyrrolate competitively blocks muscarinic receptors, inhibiting cholinergic transmission and reducing sweat and salivary secretion.[1] Sweat glands are supplied by sympathetic fibres that signal through acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, which is why anticholinergics reduce sweating.[3]

As a quaternary compound it crosses the blood-brain barrier and the placenta less readily than atropine, so central effects are limited. About 85 percent is excreted by the kidneys, and the elimination half-life is about 0.6 to 1.2 hours.[1][4]

The compound is the bromide salt of the glycopyrronium cation (glycopyrronium is the international name and glycopyrrolate the US name), with the formula C19H28BrNO3 and a molar mass of about 398 g/mol.[1]

Common effects include dry mouth, constipation, urinary hesitancy or retention, blurred vision, tachycardia, flushing, nasal congestion and headache.[1][6] Wikipedia's hyperhidrosis article lists dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation and visual disturbances as typical of anticholinergics as a group.[2] The AAD adds drowsiness, light sensitivity from dilated pupils and trouble emptying the bladder, and warns that reduced sweating can impair cooling, with fever or heat stroke possible in hot conditions.[7] The US label warns of acute angle-closure glaucoma in susceptible patients, drowsiness or blurred vision, and heat prostration due to decreased sweating.[6]

A registered phase 1 study of glycopyrrolate for antidepressant-induced excessive sweating (AIDES-G) was terminated after enrolling 5 participants.[8] A phase 2 dose-ranging study in 198 people with axillary hyperhidrosis has been registered and completed.[9] Most large published trials of glycopyrrolate concern COPD inhalers, anaesthesia and drooling. A network meta-analysis of 33 randomised trials (1,958 participants) of treatments for antipsychotic-related drooling is among the larger bodies of evidence for glycopyrrolate's secretion-reducing effect in a different condition.[10]

Most formal trials of glycopyrronium for sweating have studied topical products rather than the tablet. The June 2018 FDA approval of a topical glycopyrronium tosylate cloth for axillary hyperhidrosis rested on that programme, and Wikipedia describes it as the first drug developed specifically for underarm sweating.[1] For the oral form, the published picture is mainly dermatology review articles that classify oral anticholinergics as adjuncts when other treatments fall short, and registered studies in antidepressant-induced sweating and in axillary hyperhidrosis dose-ranging.[3][5][8][9]

After its 1961 debut for peptic ulcer, intravenous use before surgery began in 1975.[1] It was approved in the European Union in September 2012 and is on the WHO List of Essential Medicines.[1] Brand names include Robinul (tablets), Cuvposa (oral solution) and Seebri (inhaled), with other trade names across formulations.[1]

In June 2018 the FDA approved a topical glycopyrronium product for excessive underarm sweating.[1][1] It is prescription-only in the US, Canada, the UK and the EU, and Australia schedules it as S3 or S4.[1]

timeline.event: Intravenous use before surgery to reduce secretions begins.[1]
Approved for medical use in the European Union.[1]
FDA approves a topical glycopyrronium product for axillary hyperhidrosis.[1][1]
